news.title: DNC to finalize controversial 2028 primary calendar, elevating South Carolina
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee is expected to vote on Saturday to approve the new order of states for the 2028 presidential nominating process as progressives and moderates grapple over the party's direction in the midterms.

In late July, the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee voted to recommend that South Carolina be the first state to hold a presidential nominating contest in 2028, while recommending greenlighting New Hampshire, Michigan and Nevada as well to go in the early period of the primaries and caucuses before the "Super Tuesday" batch of primaries on March 7, 2028.

The party is expected to give a final vote on Saturday, during its scheduled meeting, to finalize the 2028 calendar order, which would have South Carolina's primary on Jan. 22, Nevada on Feb. 1, New Hampshire on Feb. 8, New Mexico on Feb. 15, Michigan on Feb. 22 and Virginia on Feb. 29.

The proposed order puts South Carolina at the top of the list -- similar to how it was the first state in the party's official calendar in 2024, although New Hampshire still held primaries earlier in violation of the DNC’s calendar. Because of that, then-President Joe Biden stayed off the 2024 primary ballot in New Hampshire. It also moves up Nevada and Michigan's primaries and moves back New Hampshire's.

The change in the early nominating line-up also signals an effort by the party to be more reflective of the voting demographics in their coalition, specifically Black voters and Latino voters in states such as South Carolina, Nevada and New Mexico, respectively.

Some within the party have praised the elevation of South Carolina as a key overture to Black voters, a major constituency within the Democratic Party, amid mid-decade redistricting and administration actions that advocates say are furthering racial discrimination.

The new order also puts a focus on Latino voters, with Nevada going second in the line-up, after Democrats lost ground with the key demographic in the 2024 presidential election. Analysis conducted by the Pew Research Center found that while Biden won among Hispanic voters by 25 points in 2020, Democratic candidate Kamala Harris only won among them by 3 points in 2024.

The suggested line-up also features two battleground states -- Michigan and Nevada -- that are critical to deciding the next president. President Donald Trump won both Michigan and Nevada in the 2024 election; Biden won both states in the 2020 election.

Beyond the regional and demographic dynamics, the states set to go first also reflect broader ideological debates within the party that have animated many races in 2026 and may be set to continue to 2028, including whether the party should field more moderate candidates in swing states to have more crossover appeal, or nominate progressives promising change that many Democrats feel people want.

For instance, Michigan being in the early window could mean that the ideological debate that played out in the recent Senate primary there, where progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed won by a slim margin over the moderate Haley Stevens, will likely continue -- and could be impacted by whether El-Sayed wins or loses against the Republican candidate in November.

Some controversy arose when New Hampshire was not proposed to be in the first spot, despite a state law requiring the state hold first-in-the-nation primaries. State party officials have openly criticized the DNC's calendar and indicated New Hampshire's DNC members will vote against it, but have been quiet over what sort of compromise they might be able to come to with the DNC to avoid the state party being given penalties if the primaries are held on a different date than the DNC’s calendar.

New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Raymond Buckley said the Rules and Bylaws Committee's July decision to not make the state the first presidential primary showed that "many party insiders have learned nothing from 2024."

"New Hampshire has a proven track record of testing our candidates with a rigorous, fair, and efficient process, yet those qualities did not prevail,” Buckley said in a statement last month.

Iowa Democrats have similarly criticized the calendar given that it bumps the key political state from the early window -- although the Iowa caucuses are party-run, not state-run, and in 2024 the state party came to a compromise with the DNC over the calendar.

The DNC has said that penalties that could be levied on state parties, such as fines and loss of delegates; and on presidential candidates, such as potentially losing access to DNC-sanctioned debates if they campaign in states out of order, will serve as enough of a deterrent for states to follow the order and for candidates to not campaign in states conflicting with the calendar.

While the Republican National Committee has not yet unveiled its own 2028 presidential nominating contest calendar, the party’s Presidential Nominating Process Committee voted in January to advance a presidential nominating calendar that matches the one the party used in 2024, including having Iowa and New Hampshire at the front of the line.

The DNC meeting comes amid many Democrats' frustrations with DNC Chair Ken Martin’s leadership and concerns about the national party's fundraising, which continues to lag significantly behind Republicans'. However, no major movement to pressure Martin to step down as DNC chair has materialized. 

Martin and the DNC have defended his leadership, citing the party’s success in the 2025 elections and renewed enthusiasm among Democrats.

"The DNC has a clear job: win elections so we have the chance to improve people’s lives. With Donald Trump dismantling both our economy and our democracy, that job is more important than ever," Martin wrote in a post on Substack in July. "Judged on that metric, our candidates’ results have been historic, with victories or overperformances in 90 percent of key races since Trump was elected. And at the DNC, we are raising and deploying the resources necessary to continue that trend and take back Congress."

Democrats also lack a formal mechanism by which to remove Martin from his position, sources told ABC News.
news.summary: The DNC is expected to vote on Saturday to approve the new order of states for the 2028 presidential nominating process, amidst controversy over some of those decisions.

news.title: Will Democrats’ Bitter Primaries Hurt Them When It Matters Most?
news.text:
As regular Slatest readers know, we usually spend this newsletter answering questions about the news. Sometimes, though, it’s worth taking the time to pose big questions we don’t currently have answers to. So after yet another bitter primary election this week that pitted Democrats’ progressive and moderate wings against each other, let’s explore one crucial question that confronts the party going forward: Will all these rancorous nominating contests hurt Democrats’ chances against Republicans in November?

Healing those wounds is no small challenge. Democratic divisions have been front and center this year. (Losing another presidential election to Donald Trump will do that to a party.) Some of the divides are over ideology and policy; in last week’s Michigan Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive supporter of Medicare for All, narrowly beat Rep. Haley Stevens, a pro-Israel centrist. Others—including Tuesday’s Wisconsin governor primary, in which the moderate David Crowley even more narrowly defeated Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist—are about which candidate is better equipped against Republicans or is advocating exciting new ideas.

Divisive primaries happen for a reason; they can help parties work out policy disagreements or stress-test candidates’ mettle. But bridging those divides isn’t easy, and this year’s primary season could haunt Democrats in key races this fall. Political science research suggests that longer and more competitive primaries can ultimately cost the party’s nominee votes in the general election. Only one candidate can win, after all, which leaves plenty of room for hurt feelings among the losing contender’s supporters—some of whom might choose to stay home rather than vote for someone who wasn’t their first choice.

Several of this year’s bitterest primaries so far also involved more than two candidates; this can split the vote such that no one gets a majority. That’s what happened in Michigan (where El-Sayed won with 49 percent of the vote) and in Wisconsin (where Crowley emerged victorious despite earning less than 40 percent). A 2024 study that looked at both parties’ House, Senate, and gubernatorial primaries from 2010 to 2022 found that candidates who win only a plurality of the vote tend to underperform in general elections relative to expectations. For plurality winners in closely divided parts of the country (like, say, Michigan and Wisconsin), “this translates into a reduced likelihood of winning,” the paper concludes.

Acrimonious primaries can hurt victorious candidates in other ways, too. Sometimes the positions they take to court their party’s base actively repel the wider pool of voters, whose support they may need in the fall. Contentious primaries often bring media scrutiny, which can expose damaging truths about a candidate’s past; Hong’s years-old criticisms of policing and Thanksgiving probably helped doom her in Wisconsin. Extended primaries also eat up resources. Dollars spent on attack ads against a fellow Democrat over the summer can’t be spent on attack ads against a Republican in the fall.

But just because divisive primaries can be fatal in general elections doesn’t mean they have to be. Democrats have a choice about whether to let the wounds of primary season hamstring their nominees. How the winning and losing candidates—and those candidates’ supporters—treat each other over the next few months will help determine whether those divides heal in time for November.

There’s already evidence that at least some Democrats are trying to mend fences. Stevens, the centrist congresswoman who previously accused El-Sayed of wanting to “blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” is already campaigning for him. El-Sayed, who called Haley “the least capable candidate in America” in the race’s final days, has since praised her at a unity rally the two held together. A similar spirit of reconciliation seems to be afoot in Wisconsin. On Wednesday, Crowley posted a chummy-looking photo of a breakfast meeting that included Hong and was captioned “Wisconsin Democrats are united.”

Not every erstwhile Democratic nominee has been so helpful, though. Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas, who lost the primary for U.S. Senate to state Rep. James Talarico in March, quickly endorsed him. But so far she hasn’t stumped for him, instead lobbing veiled criticisms of Talarico’s efforts to win over Black voters. There’s some evidence that Crockett’s reticence may be having an effect. An Emerson College poll on Thursday found Talarico slightly lagging among Black voters compared to Texas Democrats’ nominee for governor.

Ultimately, though, it’ll be up to Democratic voters, not just elected officials, to decide if they want to forgive and forget enough for their party’s battle-scarred nominees to win this fall. Republicans, meanwhile, are trying their best to prevent that. In Michigan, after some Democratic voters threatened to withhold their support from El-Sayed over his decision to campaign with controversial progressive activist Hasan Piker, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Senate nominee there, urged them to join his campaign. “You have a home with us,” Rogers said. Last week, Michael LaRosa, a former Jill Biden spokesman who harshly criticizes his party’s left flank, appeared to endorse the idea of Democrats voting for Rogers.

You get six letters that you must turn into as many words of four letters or more as you can; as you create words, you’ll uncover fun little asides and notes. For every fifth word, you’ll get thrown a new pair (pear!) of letters that you must combine with your existing set to make the longest word you possibly can. Give it a try!

news.title: Judge drops Nevada case against electors accused of forging certificate in 2020 election
news.text:
LAS VEGAS — The yearslong case against six Nevada Republicans who were accused of submitting a bogus certificate that falsely declared Donald Trump the winner of the state's 2020 presidential election has been dismissed, a judge ruled Thursday.

The dismissal marks the latest setback in swing states' efforts to prosecute fake electors who tried to keep Trump in the White House after he lost to Joe Biden in 2020.

Three other fake elector cases in Arizona, Michigan and Georgia have been dismissed. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes recently dismissed her office's criminal case but vowed to bring it back to a grand jury in hopes of securing another indictment. The dismissal was a legal maneuver aimed at getting around a deadline for starting new grand jury proceedings after Mayes lost an appeal earlier in June.

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is also running for governor as a Democrat, brought charges relating to forgery and "offering a false instrument for filing or record" against the six Nevada Republicans, who pleaded not guilty.

His office plans to appeal the ruling.

The defendants included Michael McDonald, the chair of the Nevada Republican Party, and Jesse Law, the former chair of the Clark County Republican Party.

In a Thursday statement, McDonald's defense attorney Richard Wright called the attorney general's plans to appeal "hasty" and "premature" and said continuing the case was politically motivated.

After the 2020 election, the six Republican electors gathered outside of the Nevada Legislature to sign a certificate giving the state's six electoral votes to Trump, despite Biden winning the state by more than 30,000 votes. The ceremony was broadcast online, and the video footage was used as evidence in the case.

The case has revolved around the defendants' intent behind submitting the certificate.

Prosecutors argue the defendants intended for their documents to be mistaken for actual electoral votes that then-Vice President Mike Pence would count on Jan. 6, 2021.

The defendants say submitting the certificate was an act of "political theater" designed to publicize their concerns about the election. They were preserving their rights to challenge the official election results and had no intent to deceive a government agency into accepting the GOP certificate as real, their attorneys argued.

Nevada Judge Mary Kay Holthus agreed.

She found there was a lack of evidence that showed the electors intended to deceive government officials, and she determined that the state failed to disclose exculpatory evidence to the grand jury.

"The fact that Defendants openly announced both their actions and their asserted purpose, rather than concealing their conduct or attempting to secretly induce governmental reliance, weighs against a reasonable inference that they acted with fraudulent intent," Holthus wrote in her ruling.

Jurisdiction had also been an issue, but the case eventually landed in Clark County, which is home to Las Vegas and leans Democratic.

The case was originally scheduled for a trial in Nevada's capital of Carson City, but the attorney general's office voluntarily dismissed the case to pursue it instead in Southern Nevada, which leans more Democratic.

Courts have dismissed similar cases in Michigan and Georgia, and a special prosecutor dropped a federal case in late 2024 that charged Trump with conspiring to overturn the 2020 election. Those cases ended after Trump defeated Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. A fake electors case is ongoing in Wisconsin.
news.summary: The dismissal marks the latest setback in swing states' efforts to prosecute fake electors who tried to keep Trump in the White House after he lost to Joe Biden in 2020.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed's Chances of Winning Michigan Senate Race: Fox News Poll
news.text: Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed trails Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race, according to a new Fox News poll released on Thursday. Rogers leads El-Sayed 51 percent to 47 percent among registered voters, giving the Republican a four-point advantage in the closely watched contest, but within the survey's margin of error. El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination in August, setting up a general election matchup with Rogers, a former congressman who is seeking a return to Washington. The race is expected to be competitive as Republicans look to hold onto their advantage in the Senate. Republicans in the Senate hold a 53-45 majority—excluding independent Senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats—and Republicans view flipping the seat as a potential pathway to maintaining control of the upper chamber. But the poll shows El-Sayed, the first Muslim Democrat nominated for the U.S. Senate, performing better among voters who are most engaged in the election. He leads Rogers by 11 points among those who are extremely interested in the election, by 7 points among those who are extremely motivated to vote and by 4 points among voters who say they are certain to cast a ballot, the poll shows. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Rogers' campaigns on Thursday night for comment. What To Know That advantage among motivated voters comes as Democrats report higher levels of enthusiasm overall in the poll. Democrats are 15 points more likely than Republicans to say they are extremely interested in the election, 11 points more likely to say they are motivated to vote and 7 points more likely to say they are certain they will vote in November. The numbers could provide a worrisome sign for Republicans despite Rogers' overall lead. If Democrats' higher enthusiasm translates into stronger turnout, El-Sayed could have a path to closing the four-point gap and making the race significantly more competitive by Election Day. The poll surveyed 1,006 Michigan registered voters from August 6 to August 10 and has a 4-4.5 percent margin of error. "The energy is on the left in Michigan, as it is throughout the country, and that should help with turnout," Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct Fox News polls alongside Democrat Chris Anderson, said in the survey. "But El-Sayed’s nomination path highlighted party rifts. He needs to reassure a wide range of Michigan Democrats — including Reagan Democrats, Jewish voters and Black voters — that he will serve their interests rather than pursue an extremist agenda," Shaw added. El-Sayed's strongest support comes from liberal voters, Black voters, urban residents and voters under the age of 30, while Rogers performs best among conservatives, white evangelical Christians, rural voters and white men without college degrees, according to the poll. Men backed Rogers by 11 points, 55 percent to 44 percent, while women are essentially tied, with 49 percent supporting El-Sayed and 48 percent backing Rogers. The survey also found El-Sayed trailing Kamala Harris' 2024 performance among Black, female and suburban voters, while Rogers is behind President Donald Trump's support among voters under 30 and independents. Trump won the state in the 2024 presidential election by less than two points and former President Joe Biden won Michigan in the 2020 election by less than three points. The demographic breakdown in the poll highlights potential challenges for both candidates as they work to energize their bases and win over moderates as the November midterm nears. The poll also shows that El-Sayed has a net favorability rating of -13 percent compared to Rogers' -6 percent net favorability. CNN Chief Data Analyst Harry Enten said in part to Kaitlan Collins on Thursday night about El-Sayed's underwater favorability in the new Fox News poll, "El-Sayed is significantly weaker than these other Democrats who are running, and I will also note, I went back, and I tried to find every single poll I could find at this point in previous Michigan Senate campaigns in the 21st century. I believe that El-Sayed being down by that 4-point margin, is the weakest that any Democrat has polled at this point in a Senate race this entire century." Meanwhile, El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel and the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has also drawn scrutiny, particularly among Jewish Democrats concerned about his views on the U.S.-Israel relationship. His past comments and positions on Israel are likely to remain a discussion point in the general election. After his primary win, El-Sayed addressed accusations of antisemitism, saying in part, "To my Jewish American sisters and brothers ... I want you to know that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters." What Other Polls Show A survey from Michigan pollster EPIC-MRA showed Rogers up 3 percent over El-Sayed with 46 percent compared to 43 percent. The poll was taken before the primary election from July 24 to July 31 among 600 respondents and had a margin of error of 4 percent. A Mitchell Research & Communications poll also taken before the primary showed a tie with both candidates landing 45 percent. The poll surveyed 672 likely voters on July 28 and July 29 and had an overall margin of error of 3.77 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: The race is expected to be competitive as Republicans look to hold onto their advantage in the Senate.

news.title: Oprah Winfrey reacts to criticism for platforming Dr. Phil and Dr. Oz
news.text:
Oprah Winfrey may admit she gave Dr. Phil McGraw and Dr. Mehmet Oz platforms but she won't take responsibility for the conservative figures they would become years later.

Before "The Dr. Oz Show" and McGraw's "Dr. Phil" daytime talk shows hit TV airwaves, they were guests on "The Oprah Winfrey Show." In recent years, the two doctors have shown public support for President Donald Trump, with Oz currently serving as the White House's administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

In a new interview with Emmy Magazine published Aug. 11, Winfrey explained why she welcomed both the psychologist and cardiothoracic surgeon to her show.

"People criticize me for Dr. Phil and Dr. Oz, because of their politics or their views. Dr. Phil, he was so practical, so down to earth, so real," she told the magazine of meeting McGraw before he was a guest on her show in 1998. "I felt that he was so instrumental in helping me. I thought, 'Oh, you could help a lot of people. You should come on my show.'"

She also recalled Gayle King introducing her to Oz before his debut on "The Oprah Winfrey Show" in 2004.

"I thought he had the language for explaining medical things in a way that was helpful to me. I thought it would be helpful to many other people. And that is how they ended up on the show," she said.

'I don’t have one thing to do with them'

Ultimately, her decisions were based on what she felt they could contribute to her audience, Winfrey explained.

"Everybody has their own path in life, and it has not one thing to do with me, and I don’t have one thing to do with them," she added. "At the time, the reason and intention behind me giving them their breaks was I thought they had valuable information to share that had been meaningful to me."

Following their TV debuts, McGraw later starred on his own daytime talk show where he welcomed guests grappling with personal and social issues for 21 seasons from 2002 to 2023. "The Dr. Oz Show" ran for 13 seasons from 2009 to 2022 where Oz discussed health, wellness and lifestyle topics.

Trump welcomed Oz to his cabinet to oversee the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in his second term. While McGraw is not a member of the Trump administration, he has shown support for the president, endorsing him at a campaign event ahead of the 2024 election and supporting his immigration policies on social media after he returned to office.

Winfrey has long opposed Trump and endorsed former Vice President Kamala Harris in a speech during the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where she urged all independents and undecided voters that "values and character matter most of all in leadership and in life, and more than anything, you know, this is true, that decency and respect are on the ballot in 2024."

The dismissal was a legal maneuver aimed at getting around a deadline for starting new grand jury proceedings after Mayes lost an appeal earlier in June. Only one fake elector case remains active nationwide, in Wisconsin, leaving prosecutors elsewhere with little to show for years of legal battles over the scheme once Trump returned to the White House in 2025.

news.title: Obama to tell ‘the brothers’ to vote for El-Sayed
news.text:
Former President Barack Obama will likely campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the far-left Democrat who just won Michigan’s U.S. Senate primary.

The two spoke after the primary, and El-Sayed publicly said he hopes Obama will campaign for him. Michigan could determine control of the Senate, and Obama remains the most popular Democrat.

El-Sayed won despite performing poorly among black primary voters. His coalition skewed younger, whiter, college-educated and progressive. In Detroit, Michigan’s largest majority-black city, El-Sayed’s opponent won more than 60% of the Democratic Senate vote. That may work in a Democratic primary. But will it work in November?

Enter Obama.

During the 2024 presidential campaign, Obama visited a Kamala Harris campaign office in Pittsburgh and said he wanted to “speak some truths.” He complained that enthusiasm for Harris was weaker than when he ran and said the problem “seems to be more pronounced with the brothers.”

Obama said: “You’re coming up with all kinds of reasons and excuses. I’ve got a problem with that,” he said, suggesting some black men “just aren’t feeling the idea of having a woman as president.”

Apparently, some of “the brothers” remained unpersuaded. Pew Research Center’s validated-voter analysis later estimated that 21% of black men voted for Donald Trump. Nevertheless, Obama will probably go to Michigan and explain to black voters who rejected El-Sayed in the primary why they should vote for him in November. After all, Obama and El-Sayed are closely aligned on policy.

Take health care. El-Sayed supports Medicare for All. Obama repeatedly said the ideal health care plan would be single-payer. “If I were starting a system from scratch,” Obama said in 2009, “then I think that the idea of moving towards a single-payer system could very well make sense.” Near the end of his second term, Obama said, “If I was starting from scratch, I probably would have supported a single-payer system.” 

Then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid called it a goal. Asked in 2013 whether Obamacare was ultimately a step toward single-payer health care, Reid answered, “Yes, yes. Absolutely, yes.”

Like Obama, El-Sayed chastises “the rich” for “not paying their fair share in taxes.” Like Obama, who said racism is part of the America’s “DNA,” El-Sayed believes racism remains a serious problem. 

How far from Obama are these “far-left” Democrats? Last year, Obama called Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani during his campaign for New York City mayor, praised his campaign and reportedly offered to serve as a “sounding board.” 

On Israel, there isn’t much daylight between the two. El-Sayed has called the Israeli government “evil,” “bloodthirsty” and a “rogue state.” He declined to directly answer when asked, “Do you believe Israel has a right to exist?” Obama never went that far. He repeatedly defended Israel’s legitimacy and security.

But Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeatedly clashed. Netanyahu fiercely opposed Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, warning that Tehran could not be trusted. Israel obtained an archive of Iranian nuclear documents that Netanyahu said proved Iran was lying about its nuclear-weapons activities and was not abiding by the terms of the deal. The Obama-Netanyahu relationship became so poisonous that a senior Obama administration official reportedly called Netanyahu “chickens–-.” The White House distanced itself from the insult, but the hostility between the two leaders was no secret.

What explains El-Sayed’s weakness among black primary voters? In 2020, he explicitly said, “I believe we need to defund the police.” Polls show blacks want the level of policing in their community to remain the same, if not increased. Blacks are disproportionately victims of crime. Tupac Shakur said: “The same crime element that white people are scared of black people are scared of. … Just because we black, we get along with the killers? What is that? We need protection, too.” 

El-Sayed wants to abolish ICE, despite studies showing a connection between unskilled illegal aliens and lower wages and greater unemployment among black workers in the same skill group. 

This brings us back to Obama. El-Sayed needs black voters who did not particularly want him. Democrats need Michigan to gain control of the senate. 

So, expect the former president to show up. And when he does, Obama will give “the brothers” a message. You may not have wanted this candidate. His positions may be against your self-interests.

But vote for him anyway.
news.summary: Dem nominee 'needs black voters who did not particularly want him'

news.title: Fox News Poll: A Senate battle looms in Michigan
news.text: In Michigan, while more Democrats than Republicans are concerned about their candidates’ ideological views, Democrats are also more engaged and enthusiastic about the upcoming election, setting up a battle in the Wolverine State. After a heated Democratic primary, progressive Abdul El-Sayed secured the Senate nomination and will face Republican Mike Rogers this fall as Democrats try to retake the Senate. According to a Fox News survey of Michigan registered voters, Rogers has the edge in the race with 51% to El-Sayed’s 47%, within the survey’s margin of sampling error. FOX NEWS POLL: NEW MATCHUP, SAME RESULT: MAINE SENATE RACE STAYS LOCKED Rogers’ edge comes mostly from greater party unity among Republicans. Nearly all Republicans (96%), including both MAGA (99%) and non-MAGA Republicans (89%), back Rogers. Only a week after winning the primary race, 9 in 10 Democrats (91%) and nearly all Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) supporters (98%) back El-Sayed, but that falls to 69% among non-DSA Democrats and independents. The small subgroup of independents narrowly favors Rogers. El-Sayed’s coalition includes liberal voters, Black voters, urban residents and women with a college degree. Rogers’ most loyal groups are conservatives, White evangelical Christians, rural voters and White men without a degree. Men favor Rogers by 11 points (44% El-Sayed vs. 55% Rogers), while women are split (49-48%). President Donald Trump won the Wolverine State in 2016 and 2024, each time by less than 2 points, while former President Joe Biden won by nearly 3 points in 2020. El-Sayed is underperforming with Black voters, women and suburban voters compared with former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Rogers similarly trails Trump’s 2024 support among voters under age 30 and independents. That’s according to the 2024 Michigan Fox News Voter Analysis (FNVA). Voter enthusiasm for their candidate is evident on both sides. About three-quarters of each candidate’s supporters are certain they will stick with their choice this fall, and about two-thirds say their support is mainly for their candidate rather than against his opponent. FOX NEWS POLL: GOP DIVISIONS SHAPE TEXAS SENATE RACE El-Sayed leads among the most engaged voters with an 11-point advantage among those extremely interested in the election, a 7-point lead among those extremely motivated and a 4-point edge among definite voters (10-out-of-10 likelihood). Moreover, more Democrats than Republicans are extremely interested (+15 points), motivated to vote (+11) and certain they will cast a ballot this November (+7). More than half the electorate is concerned El-Sayed’s positions on the issues are too extreme (54%) and that Rogers is too close to Trump (51%). Voters on both sides of the aisle share concerns about their candidate’s ideological positioning. Twice as many Democrats are concerned El-Sayed is too extreme (30%) as Republicans are that Rogers is too close to Trump (14%). By a 10-point margin, more independents are concerned about Rogers’ ties to Trump than El-Sayed’s issue positions (58% vs. 48%). Trump’s favorable rating is underwater by 19 points in Michigan (40% favorable, 59% unfavorable). Both Senate candidates also have negative ratings, with El-Sayed (-13 points) faring worse than Rogers (-6). The two major political parties are viewed negatively. The Republican Party has a -12 net favorable rating while the Democratic Party is at -13. "The energy is on the left in Michigan, as it is throughout the country, and that should help with turnout," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who helps conduct Fox News polls with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But El-Sayed’s nomination path highlighted party rifts. He needs to reassure a wide range of Michigan Democrats — including Reagan Democrats, Jewish voters and Black voters — that he will serve their interests rather than pursue an extremist agenda." The MAGA movement is viewed more favorably than the DSA by 10 points (40% vs. 30%). However, more voters have strongly unfavorable views of MAGA than DSA (45% vs. 37%). Inflation is the top issue in the Michigan Senate race at 38%, and economic anxiety remains palpable, with 4 in 10 saying they are falling behind financially. Other voter priorities are immigration/border security and healthcare (14% each) and political divisions (11%). El-Sayed stays competitive thanks to voters who prioritize inflation (+10 points), healthcare (+47) and political divisions (+5), while most immigration voters prefer Rogers (+82). Those who say they are falling behind financially also back El-Sayed by 24 points. By an 11-point margin, Michiganders oppose the U.S. continuing to provide military aid to the Israeli government (44% favor vs. 55% oppose). Those favoring aid back Rogers by 45 points, while those opposed prefer El-Sayed by 29 points. Turning to the governor’s race … With Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer term-limited, Michigan’s gubernatorial seat is up for grabs. The Fox News poll finds Democrat Jocelyn Benson has the advantage over Republican John James by 5 points in the governor’s contest (52% vs. 47%). The results fall within the survey’s margin of sampling error. Compared with El-Sayed, Benson draws greater support among non-DSA Democrats and independents: 81% favor Benson in the governor’s race vs. 69% for El-Sayed in the Senate race. There is some ticket-splitting with Rogers’ backers nearly three times as likely to cross over for Benson as El-Sayed supporters are to back James (14% vs. 5%). Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (103) and cellphones (654) or completed the survey online after receiving a text message (249). news.text:
Martin also faced heavy criticism for the handling of an incomplete 2024 election autopsy that answered few questions about former Vice President Kamala Harris’s loss to President Donald Trump.

Two months after the shelved autopsy report was released, revelations that Martin threw a phone at the desk of a junior staffer, asked vendors not to bill the DNC until after the midterm elections, and used DNC headquarters as collateral for a $15 million line of credit reignited calls from Democrats outside the committee for Martin to resign.

Democrats have overperformed in the majority of state and federal elections since Trump began his second term. In April, Democrats expanded their majority on Wisconsin’s Supreme Court. The next month, they held on to control of the Michigan state Senate.

Yet the party remains deeply divided over how to rebuild after its 2024 losses. An insurgent socialist wing, led by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has toppled several incumbent Democrats this midterm cycle. Tensions over U.S. support for Israel continue to dominate the primaries.

DNC FACES QUESTIONS OF RELEVANCY IN WAKE OF KEN MARTIN’S SCANDALS

In Michigan, progressive Abdul el Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI) for the Democratic Senate nomination after regularly criticizing Israel and accusing it of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent millions of dollars unsuccessfully opposing el Sayed’s bid against the pro-Israel Stevens.

Those divisions have also spilled into the DNC itself.

Ron Harris, cochair of the DNC resolutions committee, provided members with an update on the Middle East Working Group’s plans. The group was created by Martin last year to hammer out the party’s official stance on Israel and Gaza.

“The group continues to meet and has sketched out a plan to hold a series of sessions with affinity groups, with pollsters, policy experts, and others,” Harris said. “And members will have the opportunities to both listen to these sessions and contribute questions.”

The party’s divisions were even more apparent Thursday during a lengthy debate over a resolution calling for the formal abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Some members sought to amend the resolution to call for reforming ICE rather than abolishing it.

“We’ve adopted resolutions to reform ICE in the past, including the spring meeting in New Orleans, we’ve also just adopted a strong resolution from Chair Martin on the same topic,” said Marge Hoffa, a Minnesota DNC member. “We shouldn’t contradict ourselves by also introducing a resolution that would now call to abolish something that we have a well-established track record of calling to be drastically reformed.”

Members at its 2025 summer meeting denounced the Trump administration’s deportation tactics but stopped short of the calls to “abolish ICE.”

At an April meeting this year, the DNC approved a resolution calling for the replacement of the current structure of ICE to rein in the “lawless conduct of federal immigration enforcement agents.” Another resolution, “demanding improvements and accountability in ICE Detention Facilities, and opposing abusive facilities” was also passed.

On Thursday, the DNC’s resolution committee approved the abolish ICE initiative in a 25-12 vote with one abstention. It now heads to the full DNC for a vote, which is expected either Friday or Saturday.

“Democrats are the open borders party,” Natalie Baldassarre, the RNC’s national press secretary, said shortly after the resolution advanced. “Their radical pro-criminal agenda puts law enforcement and the public at risk. President Trump secured our border, deported violent criminal aliens, and delivered the lowest murder rate in 125 years. If Democrats had any backbone they’d vote down this dangerous proposal and put American citizens first.”

DNC members noted that the resolution is not legally binding but more of a symbolic tool for the Democratic base.

“At the end of the day, this is a resolution passed by the Democratic National Committee,” said Harini Krishnan, a California DNC member. “It does not have any legal binding on the DHS, but what it does do is send a message to voters who have moved left on this issue; it doesn’t matter what state you live in in this country. Voters are asking for us to hold ICE accountable and ICE out. … This resolution is exactly what we need to send a message that, as a Democratic National Committee, we do not stand for this.”

The DNC declined to comment when asked by the Washington Examiner.

DNC PANEL ADVANCES SOUTH CAROLINA AS FIRST STATE IN THE 2028 PRIMARY CALENDAR

John McCarthy, a New Jersey DNC member, defended the debate to the Washington Examiner, saying that “public support for ICE drop kind of across the board.”

“This is something where I think that voters certainly said immigration was an issue that they cared about,” he said. “What the Trump administration has done, especially in some of these cities where they have just been agitators, you know, people didn’t vote for that either.”
news.summary: The Democratic National Committee‘s summer meeting kicked off Thursday in Texas with members rallying around embattled Chairman Ken Martin even as the party wrestles with financial problems and ideological divisions ahead of the midterm elections. news.title: Drama breaks out at DNC over plan to ban ranked choice voting in Dem elections
news.text:
WASHINGTON – Nancy Pelosi’s daughter and Rep. Jamie Raskin are going scorched earth on the Democratic Party for trying to do away with a bizarre style of voting designed to help the underdog candidate and used in New York City.

The Democratic National Committee gathered in Austin Thursday to spend the weekend setting up rules for the next few rounds of elections, including a presidential primary calendar that could favor Kamala Harris and voting on a proposal to ban ranked-choice voting.

The controversy comes amid a Democratic identity crisis. The midterm primaries have exposed the divide between the vocal left wing and the establishment standard-bearers. President Trump and Republicans have taken advantage of the confusion to paint Democrats as led by communists – a critique likely to stay in place through the 2028 election.

Ranked choice voting is a complicated system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference: first, second, third, and so forth.

Raskin, D-Md., said the practice allows the party to be in closer contact with voters, a fear he’s addressed as he travels this summer. 

He wrote on social media he’s getting questions about whether the party “has lost touch with the Democratic grassroots engaged in the fight against Trump and MAGA. I try to assure people that our party leaders are working hard to bolster all the sensational action taking place at the state and local level.”

Advocates say ranked choice voting – used statewide in Maine and Alaska and in large urban areas like Washington DC and New York City – allows for greater choice.

“This effort is not only an attack on the right of Democratic state parties to make their own rules and respond to their own constituents, but it also moves us in exactly the wrong direction in promoting electoral democracy,” Raskin said of attempts to ban the practice.

Christine Pelosi, the daughter of the former speaker and one of 452 voting members of the DNC, vowed to vote against the proposed ban.

“We need radical transparency to restore trust. This ain’t it!,” she wrote on X.

In 2019, New York City voters approved a ballot measure that uses ranked choice voting in certain elections, allowing New Yorkers to rank their top five candidates from first to last choice in all primary and special elections for Mayor, Comptroller, Public Advocate, Borough President and City Council.

But critics complain ranked voting is complicated and expensive. Plus, the candidate with the most votes can lose.

For example, in a 2018 Congressional election in Maine, candidate Bruce Poliquin led in the first round with a plurality – 45.6% – among four candidates. But, without a clear majority winner, ranked choice eliminations were implemented.

About 8% of the vote had gone to candidates who weren’t viable so those were eliminated and the votes shifted to the second choice. Poliquin ended up with 49.5% of the vote, but the winner was Jared Golden with 50.5%.

Proponents argue the system worked – the electorate’s preference was better represented. Opponents say voting should be simpler: those with the most votes win.

Also, in ranked voting, a person’s vote may not count at all. If all of the candidates a voter ranks are eliminated, then their vote is considered “exhausted” and doesn’t go toward any candidate. 

That’s not the only drama happening inside the Austin Hilton where party members are gathered.

Democrats are preparing to finalize their primary calendar for the 2028 presidential election, knocking New Hampshire out of its first-in-the-nation status and elevating South Carolina to the top spot. 

The move could give a boost to former Vice President Harris if she makes another presidential bid. South Carolina’s bloc of black voters would have an outsized influence in naming the Democratic nominee, particularly with no frontrunner aiming for the job.

The calendar sets South Carolina as the first primary on Jan. 22, followed by Nevada on Feb. 1. New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia would round out the early states, voting throughout February.

The party’s Rules and Bylaws committee gave preliminary approval to the calendar last month. Now the entire DNC needs to approve it and the ranked choice voting ban.

Saturday is expected to be the big showdown.
news.summary: Nancy Pelosi’s daughter and Rep. Jamie Raskin are calling out the Democratic Party for trying to do away with a bizarre voting system, used in New York City, designed to help the underdog candidate.
news.author: Emily Goodin

news.title: Former Vikings captain Jack Brewer reacts to Abdul El-Sayed's Senate primary victory in Michigan
news.text: Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brewer described Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary as a "warning shot to America," while praising Michele Tafoya as a credible conservative capable of winning over Minnesota Democrats and independent voters. "It’s good when you see the darkness before you," Brewer said when asked about El-Sayed. "You see exactly what we’re up against as Americans when we have our major cities, major states, with folks like this winning primaries on the verge of having control of populations of that size. "I mean, it’s scary, man," he continued. "It should be a warning shot to America, a warning shot of really where our country is." 2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN Brewer said President Donald Trump’s election victory did not eliminate the political and cultural problems he sees across the country. "When President Trump won the election, it didn’t fix everything," he said. "We’ve got a lot, lot of things to fix. And it’s pretty scary when you start to see these radical leftists starting to gain more and more power across the country." El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit public health director, narrowly defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. He will face Republican Mike Rogers in November. El-Sayed ran on a progressive platform that includes Medicare-for-all, higher taxes on billionaire wealth, campaign finance reform and an end to unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel. Brewer acknowledged he had not closely followed El-Sayed before the primary campaign entered its final stages. "Man, I didn’t know much about him to be honest with you," Brewer said. "As the election became closer and closer, you started to hear and see stories and hear the things that he says." Brewer did not identify a particular El-Sayed policy or statement that concerned him. "All I can think about is radical, right? And confused," Brewer said. "It just seems like everything that comes out of his mouth is confusion. "If he’s speaking confusion, that means we have a voting populace that’s confused themselves to be following a guy like this." On another note, Brewer was happy to see Tafoya’s victory in Minnesota’s Republican U.S. Senate primary. El-Sayed’s victory occurred in Michigan, not Minnesota. He is not running against Tafoya. The two races were discussed together as examples of the broader national battle between progressive and conservative candidates in the 2026 midterms. "I was very happy," he said. "Michele Tafoya, who’s a friend and someone that I highly, highly respect, it’s good to see grounded conservative voices stepping up in that state." Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter, won the Republican primary with 52.07% of the vote. Former Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze finished second with 23.96%, while former NBA player Royce White placed third with 11.15%, according to unofficial results from the Minnesota secretary of state. Tafoya will face Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who defeated U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in the DFL primary. "To see someone like herself, and someone that has a name and credibility, is important, especially being a Republican," Brewer said. "You have the cards stacked against you in a lot of ways in a state like Minnesota." No Republican has won a statewide election in Minnesota since 2006. Kamala Harris carried the state in the 2024 presidential election with 50.92% of the vote, compared with Trump’s 46.68%. Despite that history, Brewer predicted Tafoya could build a coalition extending beyond the Republican base. "I think she has a chance to bring over enough Democratic voters and independents to win that election," he said. "So, I’m praying for her." Former NBA player Royce White, who unsuccessfully challenged Tafoya in the Republican primary, also recently announced his plans to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft. Brewer said he had met White several times and respected his effort to challenge the WNBA’s approach to transgender eligibility. THE WNBA HAS LIMITED OPTIONS AFTER TWO MEN DECLARED FOR THE DRAFT, AND THOSE OPTIONS AREN'T GREAT "I’ve met Royce on a couple occasions," Brewer said. "A lot of respect for him." White and former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom have announced plans to seek entry into the 2027 WNBA Draft. Their announcements are intended to test — or protest —t he league’s eligibility rules by claiming that they identify as women for professional basketball purposes. "I think what he’s doing and Enes is doing is they’re trying to stand up for women," Brewer said. The league has not declared White or Freedom eligible. It said this week there were "no immediate eligibility matters" affecting the WNBA and denounced what it called bad-faith attempts to use the subject to demean or marginalize others. The WNBA has not adopted a publicly available policy saying that surgery qualifies an athlete for the league. Medical organizations also note that transgender identity does not require surgery and that many transgender people never seek surgical treatment. Message to Vikings fans: ‘Enough is enough’ Asked what he would tell Vikings fans before the midterm elections, Brewer urged them to reject Minnesota’s current political leadership. "Stop supporting foolishness," he said. "Enough is enough." Brewer pointed to his own history in the state. He attended the University of Minnesota before playing for the Vikings and three other NFL teams. "I lived in Minnesota for a long time," he said. "I grew up a Vikings fan before I even got a chance to go play there. I went to the University of Minnesota, some of the greatest years of my life. "People have common sense in Minnesota," Brewer continued. "My message to Minnesota is use the common sense that you have. "Stop letting these people that have mental health issues represent you," he said. "You have people that are psychologically not there, and you’re allowing them to represent the state of Minnesota." Brewer did not identify which officeholders he meant or provide evidence supporting that characterization. At the same time, he praised Vikings fans as some of the most welcoming people he encountered during his professional football career. "I played for four NFL teams, and there is nothing like a Minnesota Vikings fan," Brewer said. "These people will have you at home at their dinner table. They will cook for you. They’re the most hospitable people in the world, the nicest, most purest people in the world. "And right now they’re being made a mockery of by the woke left," he added. "I wouldn’t even call them progressive, because they’re not progressive. There’s nothing about progress associated with these leftists. They’ve lost their minds." news.title: Dems turn on Gavin Newsom in Michigan as his visit is brutally panned
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom made the trek to Michigan in his effort to help Democrats retake power in Washington, but that trip seems to have landed with a thud with some would-be allies in his expected presidential bid, according to an on-the-ground report.

One key Dem power broker sniped that she “did not get a call” from the globetrotting gov and another took a veiled swipe at Newsom’s aggressive auto regulations, telling a Politico reporter: “I’m a car girl.” 

The Democratic governor is widely expected to run for the White House in 2028, and Michigan is a key early battleground on the primary calendar. 

Newsom spent time this week in campaigning for down-ballot Democrats in the midwest state, including a meetup with far-left U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, visits to a black church and barbeque event, and a canvassing speech for statehouse Democrats.

But the week was also marred by botched meetings and fundraisers, Politico reported.

Newsom apparently did not meet with Virgie Rollins, the influential chair for the Democratic National Committee’s Black Caucus, despite a liaison reportedly inviting Rollins to a chat.

“Every Democratic president that has won an election has been in my house,” Rollins said. “I did not hear from him. I did not get a call.”

State powerbroker Rep. Debbie Dingell also told Politico that she didn’t hear from Newsom.

“I didn’t hear from the governor. I didn’t expect to: I’m a car girl,” she said, apparently referring to California’s push for fuel emission standards that disproportionately affect the Detroit-heavy car industry.

Newsom attempted to arrange a meeting with Shawn Fain, the United Auto Workers’ president and a key labor figure, but that failed to happen, sources told Politico.

Two fundraisers were also cancelled. Newsom withdrew from one with state attorney general nominee Eli Savit after he found out fundraising host Kelly Neumann, who’s made controversial remarks, would be part of it.

Another event for statehouse Democrats was derailed, with the hosts citing a “small donor base.”

Ultimately, one insider told Politico that Newsom’s trip was just a “B-minus.”

Newsom’s team has portrayed his visit as a success and also promised to schedule meet-ups with some of the people whom he didn’t meet with, such as Rollins. They’ve noted his packed schedule where he met with many Michigan figures, such as Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

“Safe to say Michigan Democrats were excited by the opportunity to meet Gavin Newsom,” one of his communications staffers posted on X with video of one of his events.

Newsom’s last known visit to Michigan was July 4, 2024, to campaign for then-President Joe Biden in South Haven. While the trip explicitly was to simply help Michigan Democrats, observers note the obvious political calculations.

“Newsom is clearly taking every opportunity to build relationships here in Michigan,” David Dulio, a political science professor at Oakland University, told the Detroit News. 

“The importance of our state in the presidential contest means it has to be at or near the top of his list of priorities for collecting political chits that he can then cash in when he needs help,” he said.

Newsom, still deemed a potential heavyweight contender, may need all the help he can get. 

Several presidential polls have shown him trailing behind another California hopeful: former Vice President Kamala Harris.
news.summary: The on-the-ground reviews of Newsom’s trip are mixed, Michigan Democrats said.
news.author: Titus Wu
